prompt.context: As part of an effort to kick start the economic recovery in NYC, Mayor Bloomberg has asked you to come to NYC and advise him on whether Wi-Fi should be accessible to all of Manhattan free of charge. The Mayor has looked at several studies and has seen some research on economic impact.
prompt.question: What would you investigate to determine whether the Mayor should implement a free Wi-Fi plan for all of Manhattan?

clarifying_info.q: How many people live or work in Manhattan?
clarifying_info.a: Manhattan daytime population is approximately 2.9 million, which is roughly 1% of the U.S. population of 300 million.

clarifying_info.q: What are the demographics of Manhattan?
clarifying_info.a: 17% are under 18, 12% are over 65. 20% of the population lives under the poverty line (32% of under-18s and 19% of 65+ are below the poverty line).

clarifying_info.q: Is there data on the economic impact of Internet access?
clarifying_info.a: In the U.S., the Internet employs 1.2 million people directly; each Internet job supports approximately 1.54 additional jobs, totaling ~3.05 million jobs or ~2% of employed Americans, with wages worth ~$300 billion (~2% of GDP). The direct economic value the Internet provides is estimated at $175 billion ($20B advertising, $85B retail net transactions, $70B payments to ISPs). Using a multiplier of 1.54, the advertising-supported Internet creates annual value of $444 billion.

clarifying_info.q: Why Wi-Fi specifically rather than other connectivity options?
clarifying_info.a: That is an open question worth investigating — alternatives such as DSL or cable broadband could also be considered.

framework: Step 1 — Utility of Initiative: Assess who currently lacks Internet access and why (supply-side gaps vs. demand-side disinterest), and determine how useful free Wi-Fi would be to the population.
Step 2 — Impact on Stakeholders: Identify who benefits (households, businesses, academic institutions) and who bears costs (taxpayers, ISPs), and quantify the pros and cons for each group.

Step 3 — Other Considerations: Evaluate alternative delivery mechanisms, feasibility/cost, political dimensions, benchmarks from other cities, and additional issues such as security, privacy, speed, and health risks.

questions.prompt: Step 1: Would this implementation be useful to the population? Who currently lacks Internet access and why?
questions.guidance: Candidate should distinguish supply-side barriers (service/geographic gaps, cost, slow speeds) from demand-side barriers (lack of a device, perceived irrelevance among elderly or very young demographics). A strong answer segments the population by current access status and maps barriers to each segment. Candidates may note that at-risk demographics — children under poverty line, elderly — could benefit most.

questions.prompt: Step 2: Which key stakeholders would this implementation affect, and how?
questions.guidance: Benefits side: households gain equitable access and lower costs; businesses gain productive workers and customers; academic institutions gain connected students. Cost side: taxpayers bear the infrastructure and operating cost; ISPs (Comcast, TimeWarnerCable, FIOS, etc.) lose subscription revenue. Candidate should weigh pros — increased productivity, equity, infrastructure jobs — against cons — ISP revenue loss, government/monopoly inefficiencies, possible erosion of industry competencies.

questions.prompt: Step 3: What other considerations are relevant before making a recommendation?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates explore: (1) Why Wi-Fi vs. alternatives (DSL, cable)? (2) Alternative access mechanisms — kiosks, internet cafes, expanded public library access, targeted subsidies for low-income pockets. (3) Confidence in projected benefits — benchmark other cities that have implemented free municipal Wi-Fi. (4) Feasibility — estimated cost, constituent willingness to bear it, political capital gained or lost. (5) Additional issues — security, privacy, connection speed adequacy, and health risks.

brainstorming.prompt: What alternative ways could the city provide internet access to underserved populations instead of or in addition to free Wi-Fi?

categories.name: Physical Access Points
ideas: Expanded internet access at public libraries
Internet cafes subsidized by the city

categories.name: Subsidized Private Access
ideas: Discounted ISP plans negotiated by the city
Device lending or subsidy programs for those without computers

categories.name: Infrastructure Alternatives
ideas: Municipal DSL or cable network instead of Wi-Fi
Partnership with existing ISPs for tiered free-access tier

categories.name: Demand-Side Enablement
ideas: Digital literacy programs for elderly and low-income residents

recommendation: There is no single mandated recommendation; the candidate's conclusion should logically follow from the analysis conducted during the case.

If the analysis shows that a large segment of the population lacks access due to cost (supply-side price barrier), and projected productivity/economic gains outweigh implementation costs (supported by the $444B annual multiplied value of Internet nationally scaled to ~1% for Manhattan), then a recommendation to proceed — potentially with a targeted approach rather than blanket free Wi-Fi — is well-supported.

If demand-side barriers (lack of devices, low perceived value among elderly) dominate, a more targeted subsidy or hybrid solution (kiosks + subsidies) may be more cost-effective than city-wide infrastructure.
risks: ISP revenue disruption may trigger legal or political opposition
Government-operated network may be less efficient and slower to upgrade than private providers
Security and privacy vulnerabilities on an open public network
Speed may be inadequate for high-bandwidth uses, limiting actual economic benefit
Projected economic multiplier benefits may not fully materialize if device ownership remains a barrier
next_steps: Benchmark cities that have implemented free municipal Wi-Fi (e.g., Philadelphia, San Francisco pilots) to assess realized vs. projected benefits
Commission a cost estimate for Manhattan-wide Wi-Fi infrastructure and ongoing operations
Survey Manhattan residents on willingness to fund via taxes vs. alternative fee structures
Engage ISPs to explore public-private partnership models that reduce taxpayer burden
